CS 301 · Meeting 10 · Act 2

An Image Is an Array

A grey image as a matrix, a colour image as an array with three dimensions, and operations that touch every pixel at once.

A grey image is a matrix

shape of grey: (501, 640), which is H = 501 rows and W = 640 columns of pixels, 320,640 numbers
darkest value 0.10, brightest value 0.85, mean 0.52

A pixel holds one number: 0 is black, 1 is white. An image with H rows and W columns of pixels is a matrix with H rows and W columns. The enlarged block is 12 by 12 entries of that matrix, grey[r:r + 12, c:c + 12].

A colour image: three numbers for each pixel

shape of image: (501, 640, 3), which is 961,920 numbers
the pixel in row 0 and column 0: [0.55 0.47 0.37] (red, green, blue)
  • image[:, :, 0] is the red channel: a matrix with H rows and W columns. A colon alone means all the positions along that dimension.
  • An array with any number of dimensions is called a tensor. A matrix is a tensor with two dimensions.

From colour to grey

A common rule gives every pixel the brightness grey = 0.299 · red + 0.587 · green + 0.114 · blue. Green has the largest weight because the eye is most sensitive to green light.

def grey_loops(image):
    H, W = image.shape[0], image.shape[1]
    result = np.empty((H, W))
    for i in range(H):
        for j in range(W):
            result[i, j] = 0.299 * image[i, j, 0] + 0.587 * image[i, j, 1] + 0.114 * image[i, j, 2]
    return result


def grey_vectorized(image):
    return 0.299 * image[:, :, 0] + 0.587 * image[:, :, 1] + 0.114 * image[:, :, 2]

Two functions written by an AI assistant to the same requirements: one with two nested loops over the pixels, one with arithmetic on whole channels.

Loops against whole channels

Correct: both functions reproduce the grey image of Step 11.

Image 7: 501 by 640 pixels
version         seconds per call   nanoseconds per pixel
loops                     0.1235                   385.3
vectorized                0.0027                     8.4
The loops take 46 times as long as the vectorized version.
  • Both functions reproduce the stored grey image. The time is the difference: about 400 nanoseconds per pixel with loops, about 8 with arithmetic on whole channels.
  • The same factor as in Act 1, for the same reason: the loop runs in the interpreter, or it runs inside NumPy.

One function for every entry

darker = grey ** 2
lighter = np.sqrt(grey)
negative = 1 - grey

A pointwise operation applies the same function to each entry separately. The picture keeps its shape; every value changes by the same rule.

Your own transformation

def our_transform(image):
    new = image.copy()               # a copy, so that image stays as it was
    new[:, :, 0] = image[:, :, 2]    # red and blue exchanged
    new[:, :, 2] = image[:, :, 0]
    new[:, :, 1] = image[:, :, 1] ** 2
    return new
Notes. One example of a transformation on the channels. The groups make their own in the Colab block.

One image is one point

image has shape (501, 640, 3). As one point, it has 961,920 coordinates.
The label of image 7 is 0: artwork.
  • In Act 1 a point was one row of the table, with m coordinates. An image is one point too: its coordinates are all of its numbers, H × W × 3 of them.
  • A point can carry a label, a value that says of which kind the point is. Each of the thirty images has one: 0 for an artwork, 1 for an image taken in space.

A batch of images

shape of batch: (30, 96, 96, 3) - image, row, column, channel
shape of batch[0], the first image: (96, 96, 3)

One operation for the whole batch

grey_batch = 0.299 * batch[:, :, :, 0] + 0.587 * batch[:, :, :, 1] + 0.114 * batch[:, :, :, 2]
brightness = grey_batch.mean(axis=(1, 2))        # one number for each image
X_images = batch.reshape(30, -1)                 # one row for each image

shape of grey_batch: (30, 96, 96)
shape of brightness: (30,)
shape of X_images:   (30, 27648)

mean brightness of the artworks (label 0):     0.49
mean brightness of the space images (label 1): 0.30
The rule 'darker than 0.35 means space image' gives the right label for 23 of the 30 images.

One more colon, and the grey rule converts all thirty images at once. One number for each image, its mean brightness, compared with a threshold, gives the right label for 23 of the 30. Meeting 11 calls a rule of this kind a neuron.

When one operation is not enough

Every new picture of this act came from arithmetic on whole arrays, and the loop over the pixels ran inside NumPy.

  • Think of a transformation of an image that you cannot write that way: for example, one in which the new value of a pixel depends on new values already computed for other pixels, so that the pixels must be visited in order.
  • When a computation cannot be vectorized, is a slow Python loop the only choice?
  • The full notebook of Act 2 asks for your example in Step 18. An assignment of the unit returns to the question.
Notes. Leave the question open. Two tempting examples are wrong: a fade (a function of the pixel's position) is a broadcast ramp, and a blur (a function of the neighbours) is arithmetic on shifted copies. Only a dependence on values computed earlier for other pixels needs the loop: error diffusion, flood fill.

A transformation of my own: a fade

fade = np.linspace(1.0, 0.0, W)         # one number for each column: 1 at the left, 0 at the right
faded = image * fade[None, :, None]     # broadcast over the rows and the three channels
show([image, faded], ["the image", "faded from left to right"])

A function of the pixel's position is still one operation: a ramp of W numbers, broadcast over the rows and the channels.
